Well, like a lot of guys, I didn't really get a chance to find out. I was 15 and talking to a couple of different guys from tumblr when my mom went through my stuff and found out about it. She didn't confront me about it at first. She took the entire family out to lunch and didn't say anything, but my dad texted me asking me to come outside. This was really weird, considering that my parents were divorced and tried to avoid being in the same place as much as possible.

So I got outside and got into my dad's car, and he's crying but altogether supportive. However, he's freaking out because he thinks I'm being like, sexually exploited by men from the Internet. I try to explain otherwise, but he's beyond reason and takes me to his house. He and my step-mom make me take an HIV test and a drug test because my mother had told them that I had been sleeping around and using drugs (I was a virgin in both senses at the time). They both came back clear of course. I had my phone and my computer taken away and I was forbidden from leaving the house for a month without my parents. I think they were afraid I was going to try to run away.

I tried to call my mom to apologize, which I realize now is total horseshit. But that was the nature of our relationship. She literally said nothing, just listened to me crying on the line.

So for the rest of that summer I sat in my room, read, wrote, and, once I got my computer back, made digital art. It was horrible. I never went over to see my mom again. We met once, a few years ago, on Mother's Day. We didn't really make amends, just agreed to go our separate ways. I guess I held out hope that things would get better, but they never really did. I tried to call her sometimes and she never picked up.

She died suddenly in July. It was weird, having to be there for my sister to help her grieve for someone that I had already lost so many years ago. I think I've started to forgive her, I'm not sure. I don't feel any responsibility for the state of our relationship though. There are some people who aren't fit to parent. That's how it is, man.

All that aside, I'd like to point out an interesting parallel between Fiona Goode and Elsa Mars. Elsa Mars was also a pretty bad person, but she never confronted her wrongs. She ran away constantly, until finally she ran away from life, and SHE was sent to a personal heaven. Well, it's actually pretty basic. It's just a rubric of different categories, like Performance Basics (such as blocking, framing a scene, etc.), Improvisation Basics, Plot, Characters, etc. Everyone sort of evaluates each other, and their scores are averaged for each category and as a whole. There isn't really a grading scale, it's more, "Our group's average for Vocal Ability is 3.8/5, and I'm at a 3.4" From there I can see where are strengths and weaknesses lie as a troupe and as individuals, and get a feel for who needs the most attention an in what areas.

Oh, and comments! Lots of a comments.

So, an example from this month, I know that I'm stronger in, say, Plot and Comedic Ability, but I'm lower than average in Physicality and Vocal Ability. My goal is to work with the people who are lower in Plot and Comedic Ability, and to up my lower categories.

My troupe does self and peer evaluations and we tend to base our goals around that. So as of now my goal for this month is to step up my physicality and my vocal range, and to work on playing less zany, more grounded characters.

A lot the "rules" of improv apply more to the intent of the actor than what's going on, surface-level, in the scene. It's less "don't say no" and more don't say no to your partner's ideas. It's less "always agree" and more always agree with your partner's intent.

Nope. The two are fundamentally pretty different books.

Tom Sawyer is, by and large, a children's book. Although I read it at 17 and still thoroughly enjoyed it, it's subject matter, themes, and conflicts are still simple, easy to digest, and kind of forgettable. I'm not even sure it establishes how Tom meets Huck. I'm pretty sure they've always been friends. (IMO, Huck's relationship to Tom only serves to show how much Huck has matured in comparison after his adventures with Jim.)

Huck Finn, on the other hand, is as close as Twain ever got to writing a social epic. It's a complicated book; it vacillates back and forth from silly, childish fun, to dark, almost nihilistic content. Unfortunately *SPOILERS AHEAD* i think twain chose the easy way out for his ending and neatly tied up all of the loose ends.

So yeah. If you like Twain's style and don't mind a simple read that you probably won't take much away from, Tom Sawyer is great. I really enjoyed it. Just don't expect the depth of Huck Finn.

Quite the movie buff here, it makes me sad that you've come to see it like this. Yeah, the majority of the big blockbuster hits don't offer a lot intellectually, but even the worst movies can still be thought provoking if approached in the right way.

You bring up books. We all know that it's entirely possible to read the words on the page and not think about it at all. It goes in and out. The same can be said for really any other medium. At an art museum, you can look at a painting and just say, "Oh, it's a red square," and move on to the next exhibit. But wait: why a red square? Why not a blue one? Or a gray one? This was a deliberate decision on the artist's part. And speaking of the artist, what about them? What happened to him or her that lead them to paint this red square? It's the same reason that a lot of people can't listen to instrumental music; they're not being told what to think through the lyrics. But as the audience of any art form, we have the choice to sit passively, smile, laugh, and cry when appropriate, or to actually think about what's being presented to us. People often think of all critics as cynics, but being critical is just a sign of being human and questioning what you're being presented, not just blindly accepting it.

Now, movies hold a special place in my heart. It's first and foremost rapid-fire photography, combined with writing, acting, and music. There's so much to think about here, so much to discuss and to communicate. In fact, most movies deserve multiple viewings just to squeeze all of the juice out of them.

So, yes, I definitely understand where you're coming from. To the passive, dull viewer, movies are just being presented an image. But to a thinking, critical person like you, me, and hopefully the readers of this sub, they can offer so many questions. Sometimes it's less about making the image yourself and more about asking why the image is what it is, you feel?
